newsitem.title: USA: Cap gains tax rate cut to 20 pct okay with W.House.
newsitem.headline: Cap gains tax rate cut to 20 pct okay with W.House.

text.p: U.S. Budget Director Franklin Raines said on Sunday the White House could accept a reduction in the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent as part of the breakthrough balanced-budget deal President Bill Clinton negotiated with Republican congressional leaders.
"There's a lot of formulas, but I don't see any reason that you need to get below 20 percent" on the capital gains tax rate, Raines said on the CBS Television programme "Face the Nation."
Asked if he could accept a 20 percent rate, he nodded "Yes."

The top tax rate on profits from the sale of assets such as stocks and real estate is now 28 percent, and Republicans have long made a reduction in such taxes a key issue in budget negotiations each year.

Clinton and Republican leaders in Congress hammered out a historic five-year plan on Friday that cuts $115 billion from the Medicare health care programme for the elderly, takes another $16 billion from the Medicaid programme for the poor, offers net tax cuts of $85 billion for the rich and the middle-class and promises a balanced budget by 2002.
White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles predicted on Sunday the landmark agreement would receive the support of most congressional Democrats despite some grousing over social spending.
"I'm absolutely confident it will," Bowles said on the NBC Television programme "Meet the Press."
Bowles said he even expected House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri, who had expressed qualms about the emerging plan, to throw his weight behind the agreement.
"I think when we'll have a chance to get down and discuss the details with him, that we'll get his support," Bowles said, referring to Gephardt.
Details of the agreement cutting capital gains and estate taxes must still be hammered out. Some Republicans are pushing to halve the top capital gains to 14 percent.

"We don't believe a capital gains tax cut is the best use of ($85 billion) tax cut amount," Raines said. "But if there's going to be one, we think it should be one that won't explode in the out years, and that it should be focused as much as possible on trying to release capital so it's reinvested in the economy."

Raines said the White House believed any rise in the current $600,000 exemption in estates, above which heirs pay taxes, should help farmers and small business. "We think it should be targeted. After all, the estate tax only applies to the richest 3 percent of Americans," he said.

House Majority Leader Dick Armey, a Texas Republican, told the Fox Television programme "Fox News Sunday" the new budget pact does not mean Republicans must forego pushing for further tax reductions beyond the $85 billion called for in the deal.

The negotiators were closing in on a budget deal on Thursday night when the Congressional Budget Office gave them a gift. It said that because of the continued strong economy, it had revised its five-year estimates of projected tax revenues to include an additional $225 billion.

White House officials said the forecast of this sum provided a cushion for negotiators to use in settling some of the most controversial elements of the balanced budget deal. It helped quiet a revolt against the plan by Democrats in the House of Representatives.
